p: Eating a balanced diet helps your body grow and stay healthy. Try to fill half your plate with vegetables and salad. Add some whole grains, like brown rice or wholemeal bread, and some protein, like fish, eggs or beans. Drinking plenty of water is important too.

Our class made Anzac biscuits for a special morning tea. We mixed oats, flour, coconut, sugar, butter and golden syrup. Then we rolled the dough into balls and baked them until they were golden. The whole school smelled delicious.

Sleep is just as important as food and exercise. While you sleep, your body grows and repairs itself, and your brain sorts out what you learned during the day. Turning off screens an hour before bed and keeping a regular bedtime can help you sleep better.

Bush tucker is food that grows naturally in Australia. Aboriginal peoples have eaten foods such as quandongs, bush tomatoes and witchetty grubs for thousands of years. Today, some of these foods are used by chefs in restaurants and sold in supermarkets.

Exercise does not have to mean playing a team sport. Walking the dog, riding your bike, dancing in your room or playing tag at lunch all count. Experts say children should be active for at least one hour every day to keep their bodies and minds healthy.

Sugary drinks can contain more than ten teaspoons of sugar in a single bottle. Too much sugar can lead to tooth decay and other health problems. Choosing water or plain milk instead is an easy way to stay healthy and save money too.

p: Reading nutrition labels can help you make healthier choices. Each label lists the amount of energy, protein, fat, carbohydrate, sugar and sodium in a serve and in one hundred grams of the food. Comparing the per hundred gram column makes it easier to compare similar products. Ingredients are listed from largest to smallest amount, so sugar near the top is a warning sign.

Sleep plays a crucial role in health and learning. During sleep, the brain consolidates memories and the body repairs muscles and tissues. Teenagers naturally tend to fall asleep later, but early school starts mean many do not get the eight to ten hours they need. Limiting screens at night, keeping a consistent routine and avoiding caffeine can improve sleep quality.

Australia's food culture has been shaped by waves of migration. Italian and Greek families introduced espresso coffee and olive oil, while Vietnamese, Chinese, Indian and Lebanese communities have made dishes such as pho, dumplings, curries and falafel part of everyday life. Today, Australian cuisine is often described as a fusion of many traditions, combined with native ingredients and fresh local produce.

Food waste is a significant environmental and economic problem. When food is thrown away, so are the water, energy and labour used to produce it. In landfill, rotting food releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Households can reduce waste by planning meals, storing food correctly, using leftovers creatively and understanding the difference between best before and use by dates.

Mental health refers to how we think, feel and cope with everyday life. Just like physical health, it can change over time. Strategies such as regular exercise, spending time with friends, getting enough sleep and practising mindfulness can support good mental health. If worries or sadness last for a long time, it is important to talk to a trusted adult, doctor or counsellor.

Physical activity offers benefits far beyond fitness. Exercise releases chemicals in the brain that improve mood and reduce stress. It strengthens bones, muscles and the heart, and can improve concentration in class. The guidelines suggest young people should do at least sixty minutes of moderate to vigorous activity each day, including activities that make them puff and strengthen their muscles.

s: Public health campaigns must balance individual freedom with the collective benefits of healthier behaviour.
The rise of ultra-processed foods has been linked to increasing rates of obesity and chronic disease.
Social determinants of health, such as income and education, strongly influence life expectancy.
Some countries have introduced a tax on sugary drinks to reduce consumption and fund health programs.
Adolescent mental health has become a major focus of research, particularly in relation to social media use.
Food deserts are areas where residents have limited access to affordable, nutritious food.
The gut microbiome appears to influence not only digestion but also immunity and mood.
Sedentary lifestyles, partly driven by technology, present a significant challenge for modern health systems.
Evidence-based nutrition advice is often drowned out by fad diets promoted online.

p: Ultra-processed foods, which are manufactured using industrial ingredients and additives, now make up a large proportion of the average Australian diet. These products are often cheap, convenient and heavily marketed, yet research has linked high consumption to obesity, heart disease and type 2 diabetes. Some experts argue that the focus on individual nutrients, such as fat or sugar, has distracted from the broader issue of how foods are processed. Policy responses under discussion include clearer labelling and marketing restrictions.

The social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age. Factors such as income, housing, education and access to services strongly influence health outcomes, often more than individual choices. People living in disadvantaged communities tend to experience higher rates of chronic illness and shorter lives. Addressing these inequalities requires coordinated action across many areas of government, not only within the health system.

Adolescent mental health has become a significant public concern. Rates of anxiety and depression among young people appear to have risen over the past two decades, prompting debate about the role of social media, academic pressure and economic uncertainty. Researchers caution that the causes are complex and likely interact. Expanding access to youth mental health services, teaching coping skills in schools and reducing stigma are widely supported responses.

A sugar-sweetened beverage tax has been introduced in several countries to reduce consumption of drinks linked to obesity and tooth decay. Supporters point to evidence of reduced purchases and the opportunity to fund health programs. Critics argue that such taxes disproportionately affect low-income households and that education is a better approach. The debate illustrates the broader tension between government intervention and personal responsibility in public health policy.

Closing the gap in health outcomes between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and other Australians remains a national priority. Differences in life expectancy, chronic disease and infant health reflect the ongoing effects of colonisation, discrimination and unequal access to services. Evidence shows that community-controlled health organisations, which are run by and for Indigenous communities, often deliver better results because they provide culturally safe care and build trust.

Health misinformation spreads rapidly online, from miracle cures to false claims about vaccines. Algorithms often reward content that provokes strong emotions rather than content that is accurate. This can lead people to make harmful decisions about their health. Improving health literacy, supporting trusted sources and encouraging people to check claims before sharing them are important strategies. Health professionals are also increasingly using social media to communicate directly with the public.
